transcript:
MEETING HEADER
Date: 2026-02-05
Start time: 10:00 AM PT (approx)
Duration: 43 min
Call type: Procurement / Legal

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Avery Johnson (AE), Markus Klein (SE), Naomi Feldman (Security/Compliance advisor)
Northstar Payments Co.: Jordan Lee (Procurement), Maya Patel (Senior Counsel), Chris O'Neill (Vendor Risk), Sam Rivera (Eng Mgr)

Summary (auto)
Northstar walked through their procurement and legal checklist for Redwood Inference. Topics included SLA uptime definitions and service credits, support response times, data processing addendum terms (controller/processor roles, subprocessors, breach notice timelines), data retention defaults, and data residency. Redwood confirmed ability to contractually commit to a Dedicated capacity start date and US-only processing for the proposed deployment. The group aligned on a target to finalize redlines and sign by end of next week, contingent on DPA and SLA exhibits.

Topics (auto)
- MSA + Order Form structure
- SLA: uptime, service credits, support response times
- DPA: security measures, breach notice, subprocessors, retention
- Data residency and log retention
- Timeline to signature + implementation kickoff

Questions (auto)
- What is included in “availability” for SLA (API gateway vs model availability vs console)?
- Can Redwood commit to a specific region / US-only processing?
- What are default retention periods for request/response logs and can they be reduced?
- Do model outputs get used for training by default?
- Are subprocessors listed and is there a notice period for changes?

ACTION ITEMS (auto)
- Redwood to send SLA exhibit draft + redlines to Northstar MSA
- Northstar to provide DPA template
- Redwood to confirm retention options and breach notification language

TRANSCRIPT

[00:00] Avery Johnson: Hey everyone. Thanks for making the time. This is Avery from Redwood. I’ve got Markus with me, sales engineering, and Naomi who helps us with security and compliance questions.

[00:10] Jordan Lee: Great. Jordan from procurement. I’ve also got Maya from legal, Chris from vendor risk, and Sam from engineering.

[00:18] Avery Johnson: Awesome. The goal today, I think, is to get through the redline hot spots—SLA, the DPA, and make sure we’re aligned on the signature timeline.

[00:27] Maya Patel: Yep. We can move quickly if we’re not stuck in the usual areas—liability, confidentiality, and data processing.

[00:35] Chris O'Neill: And I’ll focus on the security appendix questions. Some of the earlier answers from the demo were good, but we need them written.

[00:42] Avery Johnson: Totally. Maybe quick context: we’re proposing Hosted API to start, plus Dedicated capacity for predictability, and then we have the private deployment option if you need VPC later.

[00:53] Sam Rivera: Right. The platform team cares most about predictable throughput and not getting throttled mid-workload. Also we don’t want a surprise model change that breaks prompts.

[01:03] Markus Klein: Yep. That’s consistent with what we talked about. For the demo tenant we showed, we pin model versions and also define controlled fallback behavior. We can do that for your routes too.

[01:14] Jordan Lee: Cool. Let’s start with SLA. Maya, do you want to lead?

[01:18] Maya Patel: Sure. Redwood’s SLA exhibit—what you sent last week—references “API availability” but doesn’t define whether outages in the model backend count, or if it’s just the front door.

[01:31] Avery Johnson: Good call. Our intent is end-to-end for the inference endpoint—so if the API is up but requests are failing due to capacity, that should count.

[01:41] Markus Klein: Minor nuance: we define availability as successful responses excluding customer-caused errors. So 4xx like invalid auth doesn’t count against us.

[01:51] Maya Patel: That’s fine. We just need that spelled out. We also have internal policy that any service credits are clearly described.

[02:00] Jordan Lee: Yeah, service credits schedule—right now it’s vague.

[02:04] Avery Johnson: Understood. We can send a clearer table: if monthly uptime falls below X, credit is Y percent of the monthly fees for that SKU.

[02:14] Chris O'Neill: When you say SKU, are you separating Hosted usage and Dedicated commit?

[02:19] Avery Johnson: Yes, typically. Dedicated is a monthly commit, and Hosted is usage-based. We can apply credits to the impacted portion.

[02:28] Maya Patel: Okay. Second SLA point: support response times. Your standard says “best effort.” We require something like Sev1 within one hour.

[02:39] Avery Johnson: We can align on enterprise support response targets. Sean—our SRE lead—isn’t on, but we can confirm the support matrix. Naomi, anything to add?

[02:50] Naomi Feldman: Typically we offer response targets by severity. For Sev1, initial response within one hour, 24/7 for enterprise. Resolution time is best-effort, but we can add escalation language.

[03:03] Maya Patel: Great. Add escalation path and named channels. Also, define Sev1. For us: complete outage, or material degradation in latency.

[03:12] Markus Klein: We can tie Sev definitions to error rate thresholds and latency SLOs. Like p95 latency exceeds agreed threshold for N minutes.

[03:22] Sam Rivera: Please do. Because if p95 jumps, our app becomes unusable even if it’s “up.”

[03:31] Jordan Lee: Next, DPA. Chris, want to tee up the questions?

[03:36] Chris O'Neill: Sure. First: are you a processor or subprocessor in this relationship?

[03:41] Naomi Feldman: We’re a processor for customer content that you send to the service. You’re the controller. We also have subprocessors—cloud providers, monitoring—listed in our subprocessor page.

[03:53] Chris O'Neill: We need the list attached to the agreement, with a notice period for changes. Usually 30 days.

[03:59] Naomi Feldman: That’s standard for us as well. We can do 30 days notice for new subprocessors, with an objection process.

[04:09] Maya Patel: Next: breach notification timeline. Your security FAQ mentions “without undue delay” but our template requires 72 hours.

[04:18] Naomi Feldman: We can commit to notifying you within 72 hours of confirming a breach involving your data. We’ll need to align wording around “confirmation” vs “awareness,” but we can get close.

[04:32] Maya Patel: Fine. Just not open-ended.

[04:36] Jordan Lee: Retention. We have a requirement that request payloads and outputs are not kept longer than necessary, and ideally we can choose retention.

[04:45] Markus Klein: For the platform, there are a few categories: operational logs, metrics, and any optional request/response logging. We can configure shorter retention and also disable content logging.

[05:01] Sam Rivera: On the demo you showed token-level breakdowns. Does that require storing prompts and completions?

[05:07] Markus Klein: Not necessarily the raw content. Token counts, latency, model id, route id can be stored without the full payload. For deeper debugging you can enable sampling, but it’s optional.

[05:20] Chris O'Neill: We’d prefer default off for content logging.

[05:23] Naomi Feldman: That’s generally how we recommend it for regulated or payments-adjacent workloads. We can put that into the order form as a configuration commitment.

[05:34] Maya Patel: And you confirm you don’t train on customer data?

[05:38] Naomi Feldman: Correct. We do not use customer prompts/outputs to train models. We can contractually state that.

[05:45] Avery Johnson: That’s a common question. Happy to add it explicitly.

[05:51] Jordan Lee: Data residency. Sam had asked earlier for US-only.

[05:56] Sam Rivera: Yeah. For now, US regions only, no processing in EU, no cross-region failover without approval.

[06:05] Markus Klein: For Hosted, we can pin you to US region endpoints. For reliability we typically offer cross-region failover, but we can restrict failover to US-only regions. If you want “no failover,” we can do that too, but it may reduce availability.

[06:21] Sam Rivera: US-only failover is fine.

[06:23] Maya Patel: Put it in writing: “data processed in the US” and “support access” location.

[06:31] Naomi Feldman: Support access is controlled and audited. We can provide a statement that access is limited to authorized personnel, and for some support tiers we can restrict to US-based staff. Let me confirm what we can commit to.

[06:47] Chris O'Neill: Also encryption. At rest and in transit. And key management—KMS.

[06:53] Naomi Feldman: Yes. TLS in transit. At rest encryption using cloud KMS for managed services. For private deployments we support customer-managed keys and HSM integrations depending on environment.

[07:08] Maya Patel: Okay.

[07:10] Jordan Lee: Liability cap. Your paper has 12 months fees, ours is 2x annual fees. That’s a gap.

[07:18] Avery Johnson: Yeah, that’s the most common negotiation point. For deals of this size, we can usually do a multiple of fees, but I need to take it back. Maya, what’s your must-have?

[07:30] Maya Patel: For security incidents, we often need a higher cap, or a separate cap for confidentiality and data protection. Not unlimited. But not 12 months.

[07:41] Avery Johnson: Understood. We’ll propose a separate cap for data protection / confidentiality, and standard cap for everything else.

[07:49] Naomi Feldman: We also typically exclude indirect damages, but carve-outs can apply for breach of confidentiality.

[07:57] Maya Patel: Exactly. Also injunctive relief carve-out.

[08:01] Avery Johnson: Noted.

[08:03] Jordan Lee: Payment terms. We prefer Net 45. Your order form says Net 30.

[08:09] Avery Johnson: Net 45 is doable.

[08:12] Jordan Lee: Great.

[08:14] Sam Rivera: Can we talk about the Dedicated commit details? We want to make sure the order form actually reserves capacity and we’re not fighting “noisy neighbors.”

[08:24] Markus Klein: Dedicated means you get an isolated GPU pool allocation. It’s not shared with the general hosted fleet. You’ll have an agreed throughput target and we’ll configure quotas so you’re protected.

[08:36] Sam Rivera: Good. How do you handle bursts?

[08:40] Markus Klein: Two knobs: burst into shared capacity if you allow it, or overprovision the dedicated pool. We can also do queueing policies.

[08:50] Sam Rivera: We probably want a defined burst policy. During peak processing windows we might spike.

[08:56] Avery Johnson: We can write that as an addendum: allow burst up to X tokens/sec into hosted, with clear pricing.

[09:05] Jordan Lee: On pricing, just to be clear, the commit is monthly and usage is overage?

[09:11] Avery Johnson: Yep. Dedicated is a commit. Hosted is usage-based. Overages are billed per token above the commit. We’ll keep it simple in the order form.

[09:22] Maya Patel: Back to DPA. Subprocessor audits. Do you have SOC 2 Type II?

[09:28] Naomi Feldman: Yes, SOC 2 Type II. We can provide the report under NDA via our trust portal process. We also have internal policies around pen tests and vuln management.

[09:41] Chris O'Neill: We’ll need the SOC report and a bridge letter if it’s older than 12 months.

[09:46] Naomi Feldman: Got it.

[09:48] Maya Patel: Data deletion. If we terminate, we need a commitment to delete within, say, 30 days.

[09:56] Naomi Feldman: We can commit to deletion timelines for customer content. Some logs may be retained longer for security and billing, but we can define what’s in scope.

[10:08] Sam Rivera: Billing logs are fine, as long as they’re not storing prompts.

[10:12] Markus Klein: Right.

[10:14] Jordan Lee: I also want to clarify the implementation timeline. We’re trying to sign by end of next week. Then kickoff for the POC the following Monday.

[10:23] Avery Johnson: That works. If we have redlines by Tuesday, we can turn around quickly.

[10:29] Maya Patel: If you can address SLA definitions, service credits, breach notice, and liability caps, then yes.

[10:37] Avery Johnson: Okay. Let’s go point by point and make sure nothing is missed.

[10:42] (crosstalk)

[10:44] Avery Johnson: Sorry—Chris, anything else on vendor risk?

[10:47] Chris O'Neill: Audit logs. We need the ability to see admin actions—API key creation, role changes, logins—stuff like that.

[10:56] Markus Klein: The product has audit logs for org admin actions and auth events. In the demo console we showed it. For you, we can enable and set retention.

[11:08] Chris O'Neill: Great. And SSO? SAML.

[11:11] Naomi Feldman: Yes, SSO/SAML for enterprise plans. RBAC roles too.

[11:18] Maya Patel: We’ll need language that access is least privilege and that administrative access is logged.

[11:24] Naomi Feldman: Standard.

[11:27] Jordan Lee: One more thing: we saw in another vendor contract that they reserve the right to change models without notice. You mentioned pinning, but can you contractually commit?

[11:38] Markus Klein: We can commit that for pinned routes we won’t change the underlying model version without notice, except for emergency security fixes. We can provide a notice window.

[11:51] Sam Rivera: What’s “emergency”?

[11:53] Markus Klein: Like a critical vulnerability or an upstream issue. But we’d still communicate ASAP.

[12:00] Maya Patel: Add that to the SLA exhibit or product addendum.

[12:05] Avery Johnson: We’ll add a “model change management” clause.

[12:10] Jordan Lee: Thanks.

[12:12] Avery Johnson: Okay, jumping to confidentiality. Your redline includes a broader definition of Confidential Info and also includes “pricing.” That’s fine. Our main thing is mutual standard carve-outs.

[12:24] Maya Patel: Right. Also we need permission to disclose to regulators.

[12:29] Naomi Feldman: That’s typical—disclosure required by law, with notice if permitted.

[12:36] Jordan Lee: Assignment clause? We need consent for assignment.

[12:41] Avery Johnson: We can do consent not to be unreasonably withheld for change of control, or assignment to an affiliate.

[12:48] Maya Patel: Okay.

[12:50] Chris O'Neill: Technical: where is your data stored? In AWS? GCP?

[12:55] Markus Klein: For the hosted service, we operate in major cloud regions. For your plan, we’re proposing AWS US regions. Dedicated capacity would be in that same environment.

[13:06] Chris O'Neill: Are you able to name the region specifically? Like us-east-1.

[13:10] Markus Klein: Yes, we can specify primary region and failover region—both US.

[13:16] Sam Rivera: Cool.

[13:18] Avery Johnson: Let’s talk about signature timeline. Jordan, what’s the critical path on your side?

[13:24] Jordan Lee: Legal review and vendor risk signoff. If the DPA is acceptable and the SLA is aligned, we can route it. But we need documents in our system by Monday latest.

[13:36] Avery Johnson: Okay. We can send a consolidated redline packet tomorrow.

[13:41] Maya Patel: Also note we require our DPA template. We can’t use yours as-is.

[13:47] Naomi Feldman: That’s fine; we’ll compare and redline your template.

[13:52] Chris O'Neill: For vendor risk, we need: SOC 2, incident response summary, encryption statement, and subprocessor list.

[14:01] Naomi Feldman: I’ll send a package with those. SOC 2 will be via the trust portal link, but I’ll include the instructions.

[14:10] Avery Johnson: Great.

[14:12] Sam Rivera: Can I ask one more about SLA? Latency SLO. You said you can write p95. Is that normal in your SLA?

[14:22] Markus Klein: It’s not always in the standard SLA because workloads vary, but for Dedicated we can do a performance target given agreed request shapes—context length, output tokens, concurrency. Otherwise it’s hard to guarantee.

[14:39] Sam Rivera: Makes sense. We can provide the workload profile. We already did some tests during the demo.

[14:45] Avery Johnson: Yep, from the Northstar demo runthrough. We have your target throughput numbers.

[14:51] Maya Patel: Just be careful. If we put a latency number, we need measurement method.

[14:56] Markus Klein: Exactly—define measurement at the API boundary, exclude client network, and use a rolling window.

[15:05] Jordan Lee: Okay.

[15:07] Avery Johnson: On the POC: order form start date March 1, correct?

[15:12] Jordan Lee: That’s what we’d like.

[15:14] Avery Johnson: We’ll keep that.

[15:16] (brief pause)

[15:18] Maya Patel: Another DPA clause: data transfers. If you use subprocessors outside the US, we need SCCs.

[15:26] Naomi Feldman: Since we’re scoping to US regions, processing should be US-based, but some support tooling could involve global infrastructure. We can ensure subprocessors for the service are covered by SCCs where applicable. If we commit to US-only subprocessors for in-scope processing, that’s something we can explore, but I need to confirm.

[15:48] Chris O'Neill: We can accept SCCs for the edge case, but prefer US only.

[15:53] Naomi Feldman: Understood.

[15:55] Sam Rivera: And just to be crystal: no customer data used for training, and you don’t share prompts with model vendors?

[16:03] Markus Klein: For open models we serve, we host them ourselves; we’re not forwarding prompts to some third-party model API by default. If we did, it would be explicit.

[16:13] Naomi Feldman: Contractually, we can state we don’t disclose your content to third parties except subprocessors under the DPA.

[16:22] Maya Patel: Great.

[16:24] Jordan Lee: I think that covers the big rocks. Can we do a quick recap on next steps and owners?

[16:30] Avery Johnson: Yes. I’ll send meeting notes today. By tomorrow EOD: Redwood sends redlines on MSA and the SLA exhibit with definitions, service credit table, and support response targets.

[16:42] Avery Johnson: Naomi will send the security package, plus propose edits to your DPA once you share it.

[16:48] Jordan Lee: We’ll send our DPA template by tomorrow morning.

[16:52] Maya Patel: And I’ll review liability language once you propose the separate cap.

[16:58] Sam Rivera: Markus, can you also send the technical write-up on Dedicated capacity and region pinning? Just a paragraph is fine.

[17:06] Markus Klein: Yep. I’ll include: isolated GPU pool, quota protections, US-only primary plus US failover, and the model pin + fallback policy.

[17:18] Chris O'Neill: Also, breach notice within 72 hours. Put that in the DPA.

[17:23] Naomi Feldman: Will do.

[17:25] Avery Johnson: Perfect. Timeline: if we exchange redlines Monday/Tuesday, can we target signature by Friday?

[17:33] Jordan Lee: That’s the goal.

[17:35] Maya Patel: Assuming no surprises.

[17:37] Avery Johnson: We’ll keep it moving.

[17:40] (Audio jump / transcript drift)

[17:42] Speaker 1: One last question—service credits, are they the only remedy?

[17:46] Maya Patel: That’s me. Yeah, we typically accept service credits as the exclusive remedy for SLA, but not for confidentiality breaches.

[17:55] Avery Johnson: That matches our structure.

[17:58] Naomi Feldman: Exactly.

[18:00] Avery Johnson: Cool. Thanks everyone.

[18:03] Jordan Lee: Thanks.

[18:04] Maya Patel: Thank you.

[18:05] Chris O'Neill: Thanks.

[18:06] Sam Rivera: Thanks.

(End of transcript excerpt — remainder is light scheduling chatter and goodbyes; Fireflies truncation/cleanup may have removed a few minutes of silence.)
